summary: Identifies uses of HTTP State Management, meaning cookies, that the IETF does not recommend or believes to be harmful. It also adds privacy considerations not covered by the original specification. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: Cookies let websites remember you, but some uses are harmful. This lists the uses to avoid and the privacy risks.

questions: should browsers let users block cookies
subtitle: Which uses of cookies the IETF recommends, which it forbids, and what browsers should let users control.

tldr.problem: HTTP State Management (cookies) is useful but has been used in ways that leak information about users to third parties or that it was never designed for.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sorts uses into recommended and problematic, forbids leaking user information to third parties without consent, advises against using cookies for authentication, and lists controls HTTP clients should give users.
tldr.outcome: It sets the IETF's Best Current Practice for cookie use, and puts responsibility for protecting browsing habits on the service, with clients only able to make misuse harder.

facts.label: Client rule
facts.value: MUST NOT respond unless user enabled

today: RFC 2964 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 44) and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Why Cookie Use Needs Guidance
sections.content:
The HTTP State Management mechanism is described in RFC 2965 and its predecessor RFC 2109. This memo calls it both useful and controversial. It is useful because many HTTP applications benefit from saving state between transactions without encoding that state in URLs.

It is controversial because it has been used for things it was not designed for. Some uses threaten user privacy by leaking potentially sensitive information, such as the sites a user has visited, to third parties. Others are inappropriate even though they do not threaten privacy.

The memo therefore names uses that the IETF does not recommend, or that it believes are harmful and discourages. It uses MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT and MAY as defined in RFC 1123.
sections.eli5: Cookies help websites remember you, but some websites use them in sneaky ways. This memo is a list of what is fine and what is not.

sections.title: What State Management Adds to HTTP
sections.content:
The purpose of HTTP State Management is to let an HTTP-based service create stateful sessions that persist across several HTTP transactions. A session may involve several server hosts, and several client hosts when session data is shared, for example through a networked file system. The session is between a user and a service, not between particular hosts.

Similar things can be done with bare HTTP and generated HTML: a session identifier can be embedded in URLs in redirects or pages, or passed back and forth in HTML forms without the user noticing. Even so, the memo lists what State Management adds in practice:

  • URLs can be shared between users without leaking the session state.
  • Session state is kept out of the URL, so a web cache need not store several identical copies of a resource (no "cache-busting").
  • Sessions need minimal server configuration and protocol overhead.
  • The user can be tied to session state however they enter the service.
  • Session information can be kept in stable storage and survive client restarts, reboots and crashes.
sections.eli5: You can pass a note back and forth to remember someone, but a cookie does it quietly in the background and keeps it even if the computer is turned off.

sections.title: Recommended Uses
sections.content:
State Management is appropriate whenever state should be kept between a user and a service across HTTP transactions, provided that four conditions hold:

  • the user is aware that session state is kept and consents to it;
  • the user can delete the state of such a session at any time;
  • information gained by tracking the user's use of the service is not disclosed to others without the user's explicit consent;
  • the session information cannot hold sensitive information or be used to obtain sensitive information that an eavesdropper could not otherwise get.

The last point matters because cookies are usually sent in the clear. The memo's example of a recommended use is a shopping cart: the user knows it exists, can empty it by asking or by purchasing the items, and the service states that it will not disclose shopping or browsing habits to third parties without consent.

A service may refuse to serve, or give reduced service, to a client that will not keep session state, absent legal prohibition. Such servers SHOULD handle this gracefully and explain to the user why full service is not available.
sections.eli5: A shopping cart is a good use: you know it is there, you can empty it, and the shop promises not to gossip about what you picked.

sections.title: Problematic Uses
sections.content:
Two kinds of use are called inappropriate and contrary to the specification.

Leaking information to third parties. State Management MUST NOT be used to leak information about the user or the user's browsing habits to anyone besides the user or the service, without the user's explicit consent. This holds even when no name or other external identifier is exposed, because the cookie itself is an identifier that can be used to compile information about the user. The memo adds that such practices push users to defeat State Management, which makes the mechanism less effective for everyone.

Use as an authentication mechanism. State Management SHOULD NOT be used to protect information from unauthorized parties, even over encrypted sessions. It was not designed for this. Most HTTP sessions are not encrypted, so cookies can be seen by passive eavesdroppers, and clients and servers typically store cookies in cleartext with little protection. This covers both information the service provides and sensitive information about the user, such as name, address, telephone number or billing information.

A "one-click" ordering service that relies only on stored cookies is the memo's example of what to avoid: if the cookies leak, the user may have to dispute credit card charges or return unwanted goods. The exception is where the user is aware of such side-effects and explicitly consents.

Some identification uses may be fairly harmless, for example where the only exposed information belongs to the service and its loss would do little harm.
sections.eli5: A cookie must not be used as a secret password, because other people can sometimes see it. And a shop must not tell strangers where you have been.

sections.title: What HTTP Clients Should Let Users Do
sections.content:
The memo says the privacy fear is less a flaw in the protocol than a failure of client implementations, and of some services, to protect users. It also admits that a client cannot stop a service from sharing a user's "click trail" if the service chooses to. Protection is therefore the responsibility of the service, but clients can make it harder for State Management to be the channel for exposure.

Because trust varies from service to service, the user SHOULD be able to control State Management support on a per-service basis. Section 3.1 lists the client capabilities:

  • Clients MUST NOT respond to State Management requests unless the user has explicitly enabled it.
  • Clients SHOULD let users review, approve or refuse a server's request to keep state, before any state is sent.
  • Clients SHOULD let users tell the client to ignore all such requests from a particular service, immediately and before any state is sent.
  • Clients SHOULD let users stop future sending of state to a service, or discard saved state, even after earlier approval.
  • Clients SHOULD let users undo an earlier request not to retain state for a service.
sections.eli5: Your browser should ask before it accepts a cookie, let you say no to a particular website, and let you throw cookies away later.

sections.title: Limits of the Domain-Match Algorithm
sections.content:
The domain-match algorithm in section 2 of RFC 2965 is only a heuristic for guessing whether two domains belong to the same service. There are few rules about how domain names are used, and delegation differs between top-level domains, so a client cannot tell which part of a name was assigned to the service. No string comparison algorithm, including domain-match, can reliably tell a domain of one service from a domain of another party.

Each service remains responsible for not leaking user information. Leaking it through careful choice of domain names, or by giving domain names to hosts run by third parties, is at least as inappropriate as leaking it by other means.
sections.eli5: Looking at website names cannot tell you for sure who really owns them, so the website itself has to be trusted to behave.

sections.title: Security Considerations and the IESG Note
sections.content:
The security section is one sentence: the entire memo is about security considerations.

An IESG note on the front page adds a technical warning. The mechanism uses the .local top-level domain internally when handling host names that contain no dots, and it might not work as expected if a real .local TLD were ever registered.
sections.eli5: The whole memo is about staying safe. It also warns that one trick it relies on for short names might break if that name is ever given to someone else.
